examples: We had a really interesting conversation about the election.
Her new book is more interesting than her first one.
The most interesting part of the tour was the old jail.
Pineapple on a hot dog? That's an interesting choice.
Well, that was an interesting meeting — nobody agreed on anything.

senses.head: Holding your attention because it is new, unusual or makes you want to know more
examples: We had a really interesting conversation about the election.
Her new book is more interesting than her first one.
The most interesting part of the tour was the old jail.

senses.head: Strange or unexpected; used politely instead of saying something is odd or bad
examples: Pineapple on a hot dog? That's an interesting choice.
Well, that was an interesting meeting — nobody agreed on anything.

entries.position: both — an interesting book, the book was interesting
entries.takes: often it's interesting + to-infinitive or that-clause: It's interesting to see how kids learn, It's interesting that nobody noticed
entries.form: -ing — what causes the feeling
entries.contrast: interesting describes the thing that holds your attention; interested describes the person. I'm interesting praises yourself; I'm interested is almost always what you mean. Russian мне интересно is I'm interested or I wonder, never it's interesting for me. Said in a flat voice, That's interesting is often a polite way of not saying you disagree.

examples: My son is really interested in dinosaurs.
I'm not interested in politics.
The kids seemed more interested in the snacks than in the movie.
Are you interested in joining our team?
We already have three interested buyers for the house.
If you're interested, call me before Friday.
The city will hear from all interested parties before it votes.
Copies of the report went to every interested group.

senses.head: Wanting to know or learn more about something, and giving it your attention
examples: My son is really interested in dinosaurs.
I'm not interested in politics.
The kids seemed more interested in the snacks than in the movie.

senses.head: Wanting to do, have or take part in something
examples: Are you interested in joining our team?
We already have three interested buyers for the house.
If you're interested, call me before Friday.

senses.head: Personally involved in a situation and likely to be affected by the result
examples: The city will hear from all interested parties before it votes.
Copies of the report went to every interested group.

entries.position: both — interested students, the students were interested; in the sense 'personally involved' almost always before a noun: an interested party
entries.takes: in + noun or -ing: interested in history, interested in buying; to-infinitive with verbs of learning: interested to hear, interested to know
entries.form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
entries.contrast: The preposition is in — not interested about, for or by. I'm interested in learning Spanish means you want to; I'd be interested to hear what you think means you would like to find out. uninterested is not interested; disinterested traditionally means fair, with nothing to gain, although many Americans use it for both. I'm interesting means you think you are fascinating — say I'm interested.

entries.meaning: Not interesting; making you feel tired and impatient. ---
examples: The first hour of the movie was so boring that I fell asleep.
He's a nice guy, but his stories are kind of boring.
Doing taxes is the most boring job of the year.
entries.position: both — a boring class, the class was boring
entries.comparison: more/most — more boring, most boring; never boringer
entries.form: -ing — what causes the feeling
entries.contrast: boring is the cause, bored is the feeling. I'm boring means other people find you dull (я скучный); I'm bored is Russian мне скучно. In the same way: The class was boring, so the students were bored.

examples: The kids get bored on long car trips.
A bored teenager is often a teenager looking for trouble.
Nobody at that meeting looked more bored than the boss.
She was bored with her job and started looking for a new one.
After ten years in the same town, he was bored with small-town life.

senses.head: Tired and impatient because you have nothing interesting to do
examples: The kids get bored on long car trips.
A bored teenager is often a teenager looking for trouble.
Nobody at that meeting looked more bored than the boss.

senses.head: Tired of something because it has gone on too long or never changes
examples: She was bored with her job and started looking for a new one.
After ten years in the same town, he was bored with small-town life.

entries.position: both — bored kids, the kids were bored
entries.takes: with + noun or -ing: bored with my job; by + noun: bored by the lecture; bored of is common in casual speech, but many teachers mark it wrong
entries.form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
entries.contrast: I'm bored (мне скучно) is about how you feel; I'm boring (я скучный) is about how others see you. bored with something that has gone on too long is closer to Russian надоело: I'm bored with my job. Common intensifiers: bored to death, bored to tears, bored stiff.

entries.meaning: Making you feel eager, happy and full of energy. ---
examples: Moving to New York was the most exciting thing I've ever done.
It was an exciting game right up to the last second.
We have some exciting news — we're having a baby!
entries.position: both — an exciting game, the game was exciting
entries.form: -ing — what causes the feeling
entries.contrast: exciting is about the thing, excited about the person: an exciting game, excited fans. It is always positive, never Russian волнующий in the sense of worrying: for я волнуюсь перед экзаменом say I'm nervous about the exam.

examples: The kids are so excited about Christmas.
I'm really excited to start my new job.
I've never seen him more excited than the day he got his first car.
Calm down — there's no need to get excited.
The dog gets excited and barks whenever someone knocks.
The study measured heart rate when subjects were sexually excited.
Doctors say it can take longer for older adults to become sexually excited.
An excited electron gives off light as it drops to a lower energy level.
The laser works by pumping atoms into an excited state.

senses.head: Very happy and eager about something that is happening or will happen
examples: The kids are so excited about Christmas.
I'm really excited to start my new job.
I've never seen him more excited than the day he got his first car.

senses.head: Nervous, upset or unable to stay calm
examples: Calm down — there's no need to get excited.
The dog gets excited and barks whenever someone knocks.

senses.head: Sexually aroused
examples: The study measured heart rate when subjects were sexually excited.
Doctors say it can take longer for older adults to become sexually excited.

senses.head: In physics, having more energy than the normal, lowest state
examples: An excited electron gives off light as it drops to a lower energy level.
The laser works by pumping atoms into an excited state.

entries.position: both — excited fans, the fans were excited; the physics sense mostly before a noun: an excited atom
entries.takes: about + noun or -ing: excited about the trip; to-infinitive: excited to see you; that-clause; for + person or event, especially in American speech: I'm so excited for you, excited for the weekend
entries.form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
entries.contrast: I'm excited is Russian я жду не дождусь, я в предвкушении or я так рад, not возбуждённый, which in Russian often sounds agitated or sexual. I'm exciting is wrong. Don't get excited can mean calm down, and Don't get too excited means don't expect too much. You are excited about a thing and excited for a person who has good news.

examples: The results of the survey were surprising.
It's surprising how many people still don't wear seat belts.
The most surprising thing about the trip was how cheap it was.
entries.position: both — a surprising result, the result was surprising
entries.takes: often it's surprising + that-clause or how-clause: It's surprising that she said no
entries.form: -ing — what causes the feeling
entries.contrast: surprising only means unexpected, good or bad. Russian удивительный in the sense of wonderful is amazing: an amazing view (удивительный вид), not a surprising view. It's not surprising and hardly surprising are the usual ways to say неудивительно. The person is surprised.

entries.meaning: Feeling surprise because something happened that you did not expect. ---
examples: I was surprised to see her at the party.
Nobody was more surprised by the win than the coach.
She gave me a surprised look.
entries.position: both — mostly after a verb: I was surprised; before a noun mainly with look, face, expression: a surprised look
entries.takes: at or by + noun: surprised at the price, surprised by the news; to-infinitive: surprised to see you; that-clause; at + person, disapproving: I'm surprised at you
entries.form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
entries.contrast: The person is surprised, the cause is surprising: I was surprised; The news was surprising. Not surprised of. I wouldn't be surprised if is Russian не удивлюсь, если. I'm surprised at you is not neutral — like ты меня удивляешь, it scolds someone for behaving worse than you expected: Cheating on a test? I'm surprised at you.

examples: The tax forms are really confusing.
The ending of the movie was more confusing than the rest of it.
It's confusing when two people on the team have the same name.
entries.position: both — confusing instructions, the instructions were confusing
entries.form: -ing — what causes the feeling
entries.contrast: confusing is what makes you lose track; confused is how you feel: The instructions were confusing, and I was confused. I'm confusing means you confuse other people.

examples: I'm confused — which bus do I take?
Students were confused about the new schedule.
I was even more confused after he explained it.
After the fall, the patient was confused and couldn't remember his address.
Call a doctor if an older person suddenly seems confused.
The witness gave a confused account of the accident.
The message from the campaign was confused and contradictory.

senses.head: Unable to understand something or to decide what to do
examples: I'm confused — which bus do I take?
Students were confused about the new schedule.
I was even more confused after he explained it.

senses.head: Unable to think clearly or know where you are, because of illness, age or an injury
examples: After the fall, the patient was confused and couldn't remember his address.
Call a doctor if an older person suddenly seems confused.

senses.head: Mixed up and not clear or orderly
examples: The witness gave a confused account of the accident.
The message from the campaign was confused and contradictory.

entries.position: both — a confused student, the student was confused
entries.takes: about + noun or wh-clause: confused about the rules, confused about what to do; by + the cause: confused by the signs
entries.form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
entries.contrast: False friend: confused is растерянный or сбитый с толку, not сконфуженный — that is embarrassed. The person is confused; the cause is confusing. confused with is usually the verb: He is often confused with his brother (его путают с братом).

examples: It was a long, tiring day at work.
Driving at night is more tiring than driving during the day.
Taking care of twins is tiring.
entries.position: both — a tiring day, the day was tiring
entries.form: -ing — what causes the feeling
entries.contrast: tiring wears out your body; tiresome is boring or annoying: a tiring hike, a tiresome neighbor. I'm tiring is the verb and means I'm getting tired; for я устал say I'm tired.

examples: I'm too tired to cook tonight.
She came home tired from a twelve-hour shift.
You look more tired than usual — are you OK?
I'm tired of hearing the same excuses.
People are getting tired of all the political ads.
He told the same tired old jokes at every party.
The hotel lobby looked a little tired, with worn carpet and faded chairs.

senses.head: Needing rest or sleep
examples: I'm too tired to cook tonight.
She came home tired from a twelve-hour shift.
You look more tired than usual — are you OK?

senses.head: No longer interested in or patient with something because it has gone on too long
examples: I'm tired of hearing the same excuses.
People are getting tired of all the political ads.

senses.head: Used too often or too long, and so no longer fresh or interesting
examples: He told the same tired old jokes at every party.
The hotel lobby looked a little tired, with worn carpet and faded chairs.

entries.position: both — tired kids, the kids were tired; tired of only after a verb
entries.comparison: more/most — more tired, most tired; tireder is rare
entries.takes: of + noun or -ing — fed up: tired of waiting; from + noun or -ing — the physical cause: tired from the trip
entries.form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
entries.contrast: Russian устал от splits in English: I'm tired from work (устал после работы) but I'm tired of work (работа надоела). sick and tired of is a strong надоело. The person is tired; the cause is tiring.

entries.meaning: So frightening that it fills you with fear. ---
examples: Being stuck in the elevator was terrifying.
It was the most terrifying movie I've ever seen.
There was one terrifying moment when the plane suddenly dropped.
entries.position: both — a terrifying moment, the moment was terrifying
entries.form: -ing — what causes the feeling
entries.contrast: A strong word: absolutely or really terrifying sounds more natural than very terrifying. Do not confuse it with terrific, which means great: You did a terrific job (отличная работа). The thing is terrifying; the person is terrified.

examples: My little sister is terrified of dogs.
The terrified passengers screamed as the bus slid on the ice.
I was terrified that I would fail the exam.
entries.position: both — a terrified child, the child was terrified
entries.takes: of + noun or -ing: terrified of spiders; to-infinitive: terrified to go outside; that-clause
entries.form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
entries.contrast: A strong word: absolutely or completely terrified sounds more natural than very terrified. Not terrified from. The person is terrified; the thing is terrifying.

examples: We had an amazing time in Hawaii.
Your mom's lasagna is amazing.
That was the most amazing concert I've ever been to.
It's amazing how fast kids pick up languages.
It's amazing that nobody was hurt in the crash.

senses.head: Extremely good; wonderful
examples: We had an amazing time in Hawaii.
Your mom's lasagna is amazing.
That was the most amazing concert I've ever been to.

senses.head: So unusual or unexpected that it causes great surprise
examples: It's amazing how fast kids pick up languages.
It's amazing that nobody was hurt in the crash.

entries.position: both — an amazing view, the view was amazing
entries.takes: often it's amazing + that-clause or how-clause: It's amazing how fast kids grow
entries.form: -ing — what causes the feeling
entries.contrast: In everyday American speech amazing mostly just means great — The food was amazing — and it is used so often it can sound empty. A strong word: absolutely or really amazing, rather than very amazing. Russian удивительный meaning simply unexpected is surprising. The person is amazed.

entries.meaning: Very surprised, often in a pleasant way. ---
examples: I was amazed at how much the city had changed.
We were amazed to find the store still open at midnight.
The amazed crowd watched the rocket climb into the sky.
entries.position: both — mostly after a verb: I was amazed; before a noun mainly with look, face, crowd: an amazed look
entries.takes: at or by + noun: amazed at the view, amazed by her talent; to-infinitive: amazed to find; that-clause; how-clause
entries.form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
entries.contrast: amazed is stronger than surprised and usually pleasant. Not amazed of. The person is amazed; I'm amazing is bragging.

entries.meaning: Not as good as you hoped or expected. ---
examples: The movie got great reviews, but I found it disappointing.
Sales this quarter were more disappointing than expected.
It's disappointing that the park is closed again.
entries.position: both — disappointing results, the results were disappointing
entries.form: -ing — what causes the feeling
entries.contrast: Russian often says не оправдал ожиданий; English simply uses the adjective: The results were disappointing. Spelling: one s, two ps. The thing is disappointing; the person is disappointed.

entries.meaning: Unhappy because something was not as good as you hoped or did not happen. ---
examples: I was disappointed with the hotel.
The coach said he was disappointed in the team's effort.
Thousands of disappointed fans left before the game ended.
entries.position: both — disappointed fans, the fans were disappointed
entries.takes: in + person: disappointed in you; with or by + thing: disappointed with the service; about + event: disappointed about the loss; to-infinitive: disappointed to hear; that-clause
entries.form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
entries.contrast: disappointed in someone is personal and it hurts: I'm disappointed in you (ты меня разочаровал). For a result or a service use with or by. Not disappointed of. I'm disappointing means you let others down — say I'm disappointed.

entries.meaning: Making you feel calm and rested. ---
examples: We spent a relaxing week at the lake.
A hot shower is relaxing after a long day.
Fishing is more relaxing than you might think.
entries.position: both — a relaxing bath, the bath was relaxing
entries.form: -ing — what causes the feeling
entries.contrast: relaxing is the thing that calms you: a relaxing vacation. relaxed is usually the person, but it can also describe a place or style: a relaxed atmosphere (непринуждённая атмосфера). I'm relaxing is the verb — я отдыхаю.

examples: You seem much more relaxed since you changed jobs.
She was relaxed and smiling during the interview.
Keep your shoulders relaxed while you type.
The restaurant has a relaxed atmosphere and a great patio.
The dress code at the office is pretty relaxed.
Some schools have a relaxed attitude toward phones in class.
Under the relaxed guidelines, restaurants could seat more people.

senses.head: Calm and not worried or tense
examples: You seem much more relaxed since you changed jobs.
She was relaxed and smiling during the interview.
Keep your shoulders relaxed while you type.

senses.head: Informal and comfortable, not stiff
examples: The restaurant has a relaxed atmosphere and a great patio.
The dress code at the office is pretty relaxed.

senses.head: Not strict or firmly controlled
examples: Some schools have a relaxed attitude toward phones in class.
Under the relaxed guidelines, restaurants could seat more people.

entries.position: both — a relaxed atmosphere, she seemed relaxed
entries.takes: about + noun or -ing: relaxed about the deadline
entries.form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
entries.contrast: Unlike most -ed adjectives, relaxed describes places, events and rules as well as people: a relaxed restaurant (непринуждённый), relaxed rules (нестрогие). What makes you calm is relaxing. I'm relaxed is how you feel; I'm relaxing is what you are doing.

examples: It was so embarrassing when I called my teacher 'Mom.'
My dad tells the most embarrassing stories about me.
Forgetting his name was really embarrassing.
The leaked emails were embarrassing for the senator.
The mistake was politically embarrassing for the mayor.

senses.head: Making you feel awkward, silly or ashamed in front of other people
examples: It was so embarrassing when I called my teacher 'Mom.'
My dad tells the most embarrassing stories about me.
Forgetting his name was really embarrassing.

senses.head: Causing problems for someone's public image or position
examples: The leaked emails were embarrassing for the senator.
The mistake was politically embarrassing for the mayor.

entries.position: both — an embarrassing mistake, the mistake was embarrassing
entries.form: -ing — what causes the feeling
entries.contrast: Spelling: two rs and two ss. The thing is embarrassing; the person is embarrassed. It's embarrassing (неловко, стыдно) is about looking foolish, not about guilt — for moral shame English uses shameful.

examples: I was too embarrassed to tell anyone.
He gave an embarrassed laugh and turned red.
I've never been more embarrassed in my life.
The company was financially embarrassed and couldn't pay its suppliers.
I'm a little financially embarrassed until payday.

senses.head: Feeling awkward, shy or ashamed because of how you look to other people
examples: I was too embarrassed to tell anyone.
He gave an embarrassed laugh and turned red.
I've never been more embarrassed in my life.

senses.head: Short of money; used formally or humorously in financially embarrassed
examples: The company was financially embarrassed and couldn't pay its suppliers.
I'm a little financially embarrassed until payday.

entries.position: both — an embarrassed laugh, he was embarrassed
entries.takes: about or by + noun or -ing: embarrassed about my accent; to-infinitive: embarrassed to ask; that-clause; for + person — awkward on someone else's behalf: I was embarrassed for him
entries.form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
entries.contrast: False friend: сконфуженный is embarrassed, not confused. embarrassed (неловко, стыдно) is about looking foolish; ashamed is about having done something wrong. embarrassed for someone is what Russian calls испанский стыд. Spelling: two rs, two ss.

examples: Teaching is hard but very satisfying work.
There's nothing more satisfying than finishing a big project.
It was satisfying to finally beat them.
Oatmeal makes a cheap, satisfying breakfast.
The soup was hot and satisfying.
Nobody could give me a satisfying answer.
Scientists still don't have a satisfying explanation for why we dream.

senses.head: Giving you pleasure because it is what you wanted, or because you did it well
examples: Teaching is hard but very satisfying work.
There's nothing more satisfying than finishing a big project.
It was satisfying to finally beat them.

senses.head: Of food, filling enough that you are no longer hungry
examples: Oatmeal makes a cheap, satisfying breakfast.
The soup was hot and satisfying.

senses.head: Of an answer or explanation, good enough to accept
examples: Nobody could give me a satisfying answer.
Scientists still don't have a satisfying explanation for why we dream.

entries.position: both — a satisfying job, the job was satisfying
entries.form: -ing — what causes the feeling
entries.contrast: Do not mix up satisfying (it feels good) with satisfactory (удовлетворительный — only good enough): a satisfying meal is a good one; a satisfactory grade is just OK. The person is satisfied.

examples: Are you satisfied with your new car?
We want every customer to leave satisfied.
Our most satisfied customers are the ones who come back.
The police were satisfied that the fire was an accident.
I'm satisfied the numbers are correct.

senses.head: Pleased because you got what you wanted or something was done well
examples: Are you satisfied with your new car?
We want every customer to leave satisfied.
Our most satisfied customers are the ones who come back.

senses.head: Sure that something is true, especially after checking
examples: The police were satisfied that the fire was an accident.
I'm satisfied the numbers are correct.

entries.position: both — satisfied customers, the customers were satisfied
entries.takes: with + noun: satisfied with the result; that-clause — convinced: satisfied that he was telling the truth
entries.form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
entries.contrast: Say satisfied with when you mean happy with something — not satisfied of. self-satisfied is too pleased with yourself. The opposite is dissatisfied; unsatisfied means a need is still not met: unsatisfied demand. The cause is satisfying.

entries.meaning: Making you a little angry or impatient. ---
examples: That car alarm is really annoying.
My little brother is the most annoying person in the world.
It's annoying when people talk during a movie.
entries.position: both — an annoying noise, the noise was annoying
entries.form: -ing — what causes the feeling
entries.contrast: He's so annoying (он такой надоедливый, бесит) is about the person who causes it; I'm annoyed (я раздражён) is how you feel. I'm annoying says that you bother people.

examples: She was annoyed with me for being late.
I get annoyed when people don't return my calls.
The annoyed driver behind us kept honking.
entries.position: both — an annoyed customer, the customer was annoyed
entries.takes: with or at + person: annoyed with me; at or about + thing: annoyed about the delay; that-clause; to-infinitive: annoyed to find
entries.form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
entries.contrast: annoyed is milder than angry. The person is annoyed; the cause is annoying: I'm annoyed (я раздражён, меня это злит), It's annoying (это раздражает).

examples: The news of his death was shocking.
The report reveals some shocking numbers about child poverty.
The most shocking part was that nobody called the police.
The way they treated those workers was shocking.
The judge called it a shocking abuse of power.

senses.head: Very surprising and upsetting
examples: The news of his death was shocking.
The report reveals some shocking numbers about child poverty.
The most shocking part was that nobody called the police.

senses.head: Morally wrong or offensive
examples: The way they treated those workers was shocking.
The judge called it a shocking abuse of power.

entries.position: both — shocking news, the news was shocking
entries.form: -ing — what causes the feeling
entries.contrast: British English also uses shocking for simply very bad (shocking weather); Americans say terrible or awful. The thing is shocking; the person is shocked.

examples: We were shocked to hear about the accident.
Neighbors said they were shocked by the arrest.
I've never seen him look more shocked.
Some viewers were shocked by the language in the show.
She pretended to be shocked, but she was laughing.

senses.head: Very surprised and upset by something unexpected
examples: We were shocked to hear about the accident.
Neighbors said they were shocked by the arrest.
I've never seen him look more shocked.

senses.head: Offended because something seems morally wrong or rude
examples: Some viewers were shocked by the language in the show.
She pretended to be shocked, but she was laughing.

entries.position: both — shocked neighbors, the neighbors were shocked
entries.takes: at or by + noun: shocked at the price, shocked by the news; to-infinitive: shocked to learn; that-clause
entries.form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
entries.contrast: shocked is the feeling; the medical condition is in shock: She was in shock after the crash (в шоковом состоянии). In American speech I got shocked usually means an electric shock — that is the verb. The cause is shocking.

examples: Hearing footsteps behind you at night is frightening.
Prices are rising at a frightening rate.
It was more frightening than any horror movie.
entries.position: both — a frightening experience, the experience was frightening
entries.form: -ing — what causes the feeling
entries.contrast: Russian страшно is two things in English: It's frightening (это страшно) and I'm frightened or I'm scared (мне страшно). In everyday American speech scary is more common: a scary movie. The person is frightened.

examples: The frightened cat hid under the bed.
She's frightened of flying.
I was more frightened than I let the kids see.
entries.position: both — a frightened child, the child was frightened
entries.takes: of + noun or -ing: frightened of the dark; by + a particular event: frightened by the noise; to-infinitive: frightened to go out; that-clause
entries.form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
entries.contrast: frightened of is a general fear (боится темноты); frightened by is a reaction to one event (испугался шума). In speech Americans usually say scared. Unlike afraid, frightened goes before a noun: a frightened animal, never an afraid animal.

entries.meaning: Making you anxious that something bad may happen. ---
examples: Doctors say the rise in cases is worrying.
There's been a worrying drop in reading scores.
The most worrying thing is that nobody knows where he is.
entries.position: both — a worrying trend, the trend is worrying
entries.form: -ing — what causes the feeling
entries.contrast: As an adjective worrying is more British. Americans more often say worrisome, troubling or, in news and business, concerning: a worrisome trend. Stop worrying is the verb (перестань волноваться), not the adjective. The person is worried.

entries.meaning: Anxious because you think something bad has happened or may happen. ---
examples: My mom gets worried if I don't call.
I'm more worried about the test than I was last week.
The doctor had a worried look on her face.
entries.position: both — worried parents, the parents were worried
entries.takes: about + noun or -ing: worried about money; that-clause: worried that he'd get lost; for + person or their safety: worried for her; by + a particular cause: worried by the news
entries.form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
entries.contrast: I'm worried is a feeling now (я волнуюсь, беспокоюсь); I worry is a habit (я вечно переживаю). To comfort someone, the usual phrase is Don't worry. Not worried of. The cause is worrying, or in American English more often worrisome.

examples: Moving across the country was exhausting.
The most exhausting part of the job is the commute.
After an exhausting week, we slept until noon.
entries.position: both — an exhausting trip, the trip was exhausting
entries.form: -ing — what causes the feeling
entries.contrast: False friend: исчерпывающий is exhaustive (an exhaustive list), not exhausting. exhausting is what wears you out; the person is exhausted.

examples: I was completely exhausted after the race.
The exhausted firefighters finally got some sleep.
She looked even more exhausted than the day before.
The land was dry and exhausted after years of growing cotton.
Crews sealed the exhausted mine in the 1950s.

senses.head: Extremely tired
examples: I was completely exhausted after the race.
The exhausted firefighters finally got some sleep.
She looked even more exhausted than the day before.

senses.head: Completely used up, with nothing left
examples: The land was dry and exhausted after years of growing cotton.
Crews sealed the exhausted mine in the 1950s.

entries.position: both — exhausted firefighters, the firefighters were exhausted
entries.takes: from + noun or -ing: exhausted from the trip
entries.form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
entries.contrast: A strong word: completely or absolutely exhausted sounds more natural than very exhausted. It is much stronger than tired — not just устал, but вымотан. exhausted supplies are used up (исчерпаны); exhaustive means complete (исчерпывающий).

examples: The museum has a fascinating exhibit on ancient Egypt.
I find his ideas absolutely fascinating.
It was the most fascinating class I took in college.
entries.position: both — a fascinating story, the story was fascinating
entries.form: -ing — what causes the feeling
entries.contrast: fascinating is much stronger than interesting, so it goes more naturally with absolutely or really than with very. The person is fascinated.

entries.meaning: Extremely interested, and unable to stop watching or thinking about something. ---
examples: The kids were fascinated by the sharks.
He's always been fascinated with old maps.
She was fascinated to learn that her family came from Ireland.
entries.position: both — fascinated kids, the kids were fascinated
entries.takes: by or with + noun: fascinated by insects, fascinated with old maps; to-infinitive: fascinated to learn
entries.form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
entries.contrast: interested in, but fascinated by or with — not fascinated in. fascinated is much stronger than interested. The thing is fascinating.

entries.meaning: Making you feel sad and without hope. ---
examples: The news is so depressing these days.
Winter here is long, gray and depressing.
It's the most depressing movie I've ever seen.
entries.position: both — depressing news, the news was depressing
entries.form: -ing — what causes the feeling
entries.contrast: depressing is the thing that makes you sad (угнетающий, тоскливый); the person is depressed. Russian депрессивный covers both, so депрессивный фильм is a depressing movie, never a depressed movie. I'm depressing means you make other people sad.

examples: He's been depressed since his dog died.
I get kind of depressed when it rains all week.
She felt more depressed than ever after the holidays.
Clinically depressed patients often have trouble sleeping.
Talk to a doctor if you think you might be depressed.
The factory closing left the town economically depressed.
Home prices are still depressed in parts of the Midwest.

senses.head: Very sad and without hope, especially for a long time
examples: He's been depressed since his dog died.
I get kind of depressed when it rains all week.
She felt more depressed than ever after the holidays.

senses.head: Suffering from depression as a medical condition
examples: Clinically depressed patients often have trouble sleeping.
Talk to a doctor if you think you might be depressed.

senses.head: Having little business activity, few jobs or lower prices than usual
examples: The factory closing left the town economically depressed.
Home prices are still depressed in parts of the Midwest.

entries.position: both — a depressed teenager, she seemed depressed; the economic sense is common before a noun: a depressed area
entries.takes: about + noun or -ing: depressed about losing the job
entries.form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
entries.contrast: In everyday speech depressed can just mean very sad, but it is also the medical word for clinical depression, so use it with care. a depressed area is not sad but poor, with few jobs. The cause is depressing.

entries.meaning: Making you feel annoyed and discouraged because you cannot do or get what you want. ---
examples: It's frustrating when the website keeps crashing.
Losing in the last minute was the most frustrating part.
Learning to drive a stick shift can be really frustrating.
entries.position: both — a frustrating problem, the problem was frustrating
entries.form: -ing — what causes the feeling
entries.contrast: Russian has no single word: frustrating is what makes you feel досадно, бесит or руки опускаются because you can't get something done. It is an everyday word, not the psychology term фрустрирующий. The person is frustrated.

examples: I get so frustrated when my computer freezes.
Voters are frustrated with both parties.
The longer we waited, the more frustrated we got.
He's a frustrated actor who ended up selling insurance.
Every frustrated novelist in the office wanted to write the newsletter.

senses.head: Annoyed and discouraged because you cannot do or get what you want
examples: I get so frustrated when my computer freezes.
Voters are frustrated with both parties.
The longer we waited, the more frustrated we got.

senses.head: Wanting to be a particular kind of person, such as an artist, but never having managed it
examples: He's a frustrated actor who ended up selling insurance.
Every frustrated novelist in the office wanted to write the newsletter.

entries.position: both — frustrated voters, the voters were frustrated; in the sense 'never became what they wanted' only before a noun: a frustrated writer
entries.takes: with or by + noun: frustrated with the software, frustrated by the delays; at + thing: frustrated at the lack of progress; that-clause
entries.form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
entries.contrast: frustrated is an everyday word (раздосадован, злюсь, что не получается), not a psychology term like фрустрированный. It is not upset (расстроен) or disappointed: frustrated means you keep trying and it still doesn't work. Before a noun it can mean someone who never became what they wanted: a frustrated actor.

entries.meaning: Funny and entertaining in a way that makes you smile. ---
examples: He told an amusing story about his first day at work.
I didn't find his jokes very amusing.
Her speech was more amusing than I expected.
entries.position: both — an amusing story, the story was amusing
entries.form: -ing — what causes the feeling
entries.contrast: amusing is milder than funny — it makes you smile rather than laugh out loud. The person is amused.

examples: She seemed amused by my accent.
He watched us with an amused smile.
My teacher was not amused when I fell asleep in class.
Coloring books kept the kids amused on the flight.
There's plenty in the city to keep you amused.

senses.head: Finding something funny
examples: She seemed amused by my accent.
He watched us with an amused smile.
My teacher was not amused when I fell asleep in class.

senses.head: Busy and entertained, so that you are not bored
examples: Coloring books kept the kids amused on the flight.
There's plenty in the city to keep you amused.

entries.position: both — an amused smile, she looked amused
entries.takes: by or at + noun: amused by the puppy; to-infinitive: amused to see
entries.form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
entries.contrast: not amused is a polite way to say someone was annoyed: The boss was not amused (шефу было не до смеха). keep someone amused means keep them busy and entertained. The cause is amusing.

entries.meaning: So surprising that it is hard to believe. ---
examples: The team made an astonishing comeback in the fourth quarter.
It's astonishing how little the town has changed.
The most astonishing thing is that he survived.
entries.position: both — an astonishing comeback, the comeback was astonishing
entries.form: -ing — what causes the feeling
entries.contrast: Stronger and more formal than surprising. Close to amazing, but it never just means great the way amazing does in speech. The person is astonished.

examples: I was astonished to see how big the kids had gotten.
Doctors were astonished by her recovery.
He stared at me with an astonished expression.
entries.position: both — an astonished expression, we were astonished
entries.takes: at or by + noun: astonished at the news; to-infinitive: astonished to find; that-clause
entries.form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
entries.contrast: Stronger than surprised and a little formal. Not astonished of. The cause is astonishing.

examples: The colors are pleasing to the eye.
The new park is a pleasing addition to downtown.
The second design was more pleasing than the first.
entries.position: both — a pleasing design, the design is pleasing
entries.takes: to + person or sense: pleasing to the eye, pleasing to customers
entries.form: -ing — what causes the feeling
entries.contrast: pleasing is formal and usually describes how something looks or sounds: a pleasing color. In conversation Americans say nice or pleasant. The person who feels the pleasure is pleased.

examples: The coach was pleased with how the team played.
She looked very pleased with herself.
I've never been more pleased with a haircut.
We are pleased to announce the opening of our new store.
I'm pleased that you could come.

senses.head: Happy and satisfied with something
examples: The coach was pleased with how the team played.
She looked very pleased with herself.
I've never been more pleased with a haircut.

senses.head: Glad to do or hear something; used especially in polite phrases
examples: We are pleased to announce the opening of our new store.
I'm pleased that you could come.

entries.position: both — mostly after a verb: I was pleased; before a noun mainly with smile, look, expression: a pleased smile
entries.takes: with + noun: pleased with the results; about + noun; for + person: pleased for you; to-infinitive: pleased to meet you; that-clause
entries.form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
entries.contrast: pleased with something is being satisfied with it (доволен); pleased for someone is being happy about their good news (рад за тебя). pleased with yourself often means too proud of yourself. Pleased to meet you is correct but formal; Americans usually say Nice to meet you.

examples: The game had a thrilling finish.
Riding a roller coaster for the first time was thrilling.
It was the most thrilling race of the season.
entries.position: both — a thrilling finish, the finish was thrilling
entries.form: -ing — what causes the feeling
entries.contrast: thrilling is stronger than exciting and usually describes events: a thrilling finish. The person is thrilled. A thriller is the noun for a suspense book or movie.

examples: We're thrilled to have you here.
My parents were thrilled with the news.
I wasn't exactly thrilled about working on Sunday.
entries.position: predicative only — I'm thrilled, she was thrilled; not normally before a noun
entries.takes: with or about + noun: thrilled with the gift; to-infinitive: thrilled to be here; that-clause; for + person: thrilled for you
entries.form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
entries.contrast: Very strong — Russian в восторге, безумно рад. not thrilled is understatement for unhappy: She wasn't thrilled about the idea (ей идея не понравилась). The cause is thrilling.

examples: The bill passed with overwhelming support.
The evidence against him was overwhelming.
An overwhelming majority of voters said yes.
The first week at a new job can be overwhelming.
She felt an overwhelming urge to cry.
College applications are more overwhelming than most parents remember.

senses.head: Very great in amount or strength, so that nothing can compete with it
examples: The bill passed with overwhelming support.
The evidence against him was overwhelming.
An overwhelming majority of voters said yes.

senses.head: So strong or so much that it is hard to deal with
examples: The first week at a new job can be overwhelming.
She felt an overwhelming urge to cry.
College applications are more overwhelming than most parents remember.

entries.position: both — overwhelming support, the job felt overwhelming
entries.form: -ing — what causes the feeling
entries.contrast: an overwhelming majority is подавляющее большинство, but Russian подавляющий fits only that sense; for feelings and workload use ошеломляющий or непосильный. The person who can't cope is overwhelmed.

examples: Nurses are overwhelmed with patients this winter.
I feel totally overwhelmed right now.
The overwhelmed staff couldn't answer every call.
She was overwhelmed with joy when she saw her son.
We were overwhelmed by the kindness of strangers.

senses.head: Having too much to do or deal with, so that you cannot cope
examples: Nurses are overwhelmed with patients this winter.
I feel totally overwhelmed right now.
The overwhelmed staff couldn't answer every call.

senses.head: Deeply affected by a strong emotion
examples: She was overwhelmed with joy when she saw her son.
We were overwhelmed by the kindness of strangers.

entries.position: both — overwhelmed nurses, the nurses were overwhelmed
entries.takes: by or with + noun: overwhelmed with work, overwhelmed by grief
entries.form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
entries.contrast: overwhelmed is not only negative: overwhelmed with gratitude (переполнен благодарностью) is a good feeling. For я не справляюсь say I'm overwhelmed, not I'm overwhelming.

entries.meaning: Causing worry or fear that something bad is happening. ---
examples: Glaciers are melting at an alarming rate.
The number of cases is alarming.
The most alarming part of the report was about drinking water.
entries.position: both — an alarming rate, the numbers are alarming
entries.form: -ing — what causes the feeling
entries.contrast: alarming is what makes you worried (тревожный): at an alarming rate. The person is alarmed.

examples: Parents are alarmed by the rise in vaping.
Don't be alarmed — it's only a fire drill.
Neighbors grew more alarmed as the smoke got thicker.
Emergency exit only — door is alarmed.
All the windows on the ground floor are alarmed.

senses.head: Worried or frightened that something dangerous or bad might happen
examples: Parents are alarmed by the rise in vaping.
Don't be alarmed — it's only a fire drill.
Neighbors grew more alarmed as the smoke got thicker.

senses.head: Fitted with an alarm that goes off if it is opened
examples: Emergency exit only — door is alarmed.
All the windows on the ground floor are alarmed.

entries.position: both — an alarmed look, they were alarmed; in the sense 'fitted with an alarm' mostly after a verb: the door is alarmed
entries.takes: at or by + noun: alarmed at the news; to-infinitive: alarmed to find; that-clause
entries.form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
entries.contrast: alarmed is worried, not panicked — Russian встревожен. On a sign, This door is alarmed means it has an alarm, not that the door is scared. The cause is alarming.

examples: His sudden decision to quit is puzzling.
There's something puzzling about the timeline.
The most puzzling thing is why nobody noticed.
entries.position: both — a puzzling question, the question was puzzling
entries.form: -ing — what causes the feeling
entries.contrast: The cause is puzzling (непонятный, загадочный); the person is puzzled (озадачен). puzzling is about something you can't explain; confusing is about something badly organized or unclear.

entries.meaning: Confused because you cannot understand or explain something. ---
examples: He gave me a puzzled look.
Scientists are puzzled by the strange signals.
I'm still puzzled about why she left so early.
entries.position: both — a puzzled look, she looked puzzled
entries.takes: by + noun: puzzled by his answer; about or as to + noun or wh-clause: puzzled about why she left
entries.form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
entries.contrast: puzzled means you are thinking hard about something you can't explain; confused means you have lost track. The cause is puzzling.

examples: He has an irritating habit of cracking his knuckles.
The most irritating thing about the app is the pop-up ads.
That buzzing noise is so irritating.
Some soaps are irritating to sensitive skin.
Smoke can be irritating to the eyes and throat.

senses.head: Annoying, especially because it keeps happening
examples: He has an irritating habit of cracking his knuckles.
The most irritating thing about the app is the pop-up ads.
That buzzing noise is so irritating.

senses.head: Making skin, eyes or another part of the body sore or red
examples: Some soaps are irritating to sensitive skin.
Smoke can be irritating to the eyes and throat.

entries.position: both — an irritating habit, the habit is irritating
entries.form: -ing — what causes the feeling
entries.contrast: irritating is close to annoying, often about something that keeps happening. The person is irritated. Like Russian раздражающий, it also describes what makes skin or eyes sore.

examples: She sounded irritated on the phone.
I get irritated when people cut in line.
He was more irritated by the delay than by the price.
My eyes get irritated from the chlorine.
Use a gentle cream on irritated skin.

senses.head: Annoyed and impatient
examples: She sounded irritated on the phone.
I get irritated when people cut in line.
He was more irritated by the delay than by the price.

senses.head: Of skin or eyes, sore, red or itchy
examples: My eyes get irritated from the chlorine.
Use a gentle cream on irritated skin.

entries.position: both — an irritated voice, she sounded irritated
entries.takes: with + person: irritated with him; at or by + thing: irritated by the noise
entries.form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
entries.contrast: irritated is about as strong as annoyed and weaker than angry. The cause is irritating. For skin and eyes, irritated means sore or red, not angry.

examples: The bathroom at the gas station was disgusting.
This coffee tastes disgusting.
That's the most disgusting thing I've ever eaten.
What they did to those animals is disgusting.
It's disgusting that the executives got bonuses while workers lost their jobs.

senses.head: Extremely unpleasant to smell, taste, look at or touch
examples: The bathroom at the gas station was disgusting.
This coffee tastes disgusting.
That's the most disgusting thing I've ever eaten.

senses.head: Morally shocking and unacceptable
examples: What they did to those animals is disgusting.
It's disgusting that the executives got bonuses while workers lost their jobs.

entries.position: both — a disgusting smell, the smell was disgusting
entries.form: -ing — what causes the feeling
entries.contrast: A strong word: absolutely or really disgusting. Russian отвратительный is often used for bad weather or bad service; disgusting is stronger and suggests something makes you feel sick. The person is disgusted.

entries.meaning: Feeling strong dislike or disapproval because something is unpleasant or wrong. ---
examples: I was disgusted by the smell in the fridge.
Many voters are disgusted with the whole campaign.
She walked out with a disgusted look on her face.
entries.position: both — a disgusted look, I was disgusted
entries.takes: with + person or yourself: disgusted with himself; by or at + thing: disgusted by the smell, disgusted at the waste
entries.form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
entries.contrast: The person is disgusted; the thing is disgusting — I'm disgusting insults yourself. disgusted covers both physical revulsion (испытываю отвращение) and moral anger (возмущён).

examples: The early test results are very encouraging.
Sales this month were more encouraging than last month.
It's encouraging to see so many young people vote.
My coach was always encouraging.
She gave me an encouraging smile.

senses.head: Giving you hope that something will go well
examples: The early test results are very encouraging.
Sales this month were more encouraging than last month.
It's encouraging to see so many young people vote.

senses.head: Giving someone support, praise or confidence
examples: My coach was always encouraging.
She gave me an encouraging smile.

entries.position: both — encouraging news, the news is encouraging
entries.form: -ing — what causes the feeling
entries.contrast: encouraging news gives hope (обнадёживающий); an encouraging person gives support (ободряющий). The person who feels hopeful is encouraged.

examples: We're encouraged by the progress so far.
After the meeting, I felt more encouraged about the project.
Doctors were encouraged to see her walking again.
entries.position: predicative only — after be, feel or seem: We felt encouraged
entries.takes: by + noun: encouraged by the results; to-infinitive: encouraged to see
entries.form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
entries.contrast: be encouraged to do something is usually the verb in the passive: Students are encouraged to ask questions (студентам предлагают задавать вопросы) — nobody is feeling hopeful. The adjective is a feeling: I'm encouraged by the news (меня это обнадёживает). The cause is encouraging.

entries.meaning: Making people want to do something good, creative or brave. ---
examples: Her speech at graduation was really inspiring.
He's one of the most inspiring teachers I've had.
It's an inspiring story of a family that never gave up.
entries.position: both — an inspiring speech, the speech was inspiring
entries.form: -ing — what causes the feeling
entries.contrast: inspiring is what makes you want to act (вдохновляющий). inspired can describe the person, but before a noun it usually means brilliant: an inspired idea, not an idea that inspires. uninspiring means dull.

examples: After the trip, I felt inspired to start painting again.
Kids come out of the science museum totally inspired.
I've never felt more inspired than I did that summer.
Hiring her was an inspired choice.
The band gave an inspired performance.
The restaurant serves Mexican-inspired dishes.
Police believe the attack was politically inspired.

senses.head: Feeling eager and excited to do something, especially something creative
examples: After the trip, I felt inspired to start painting again.
Kids come out of the science museum totally inspired.
I've never felt more inspired than I did that summer.

senses.head: Extremely good or clever, as if done with special talent
examples: Hiring her was an inspired choice.
The band gave an inspired performance.

senses.head: Influenced by a particular style, place or idea; usually joined to another word with a hyphen
examples: The restaurant serves Mexican-inspired dishes.
Police believe the attack was politically inspired.

entries.position: both — I feel inspired; before a noun it usually means very good: an inspired choice
entries.takes: by + noun: inspired by her story; to-infinitive: inspired to write
entries.form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
entries.contrast: The meaning changes with position: She felt inspired (вдохновлённая) is about the person, but an inspired choice or an inspired performance means brilliant (блестящий, удачный). inspired by + a source after a noun is often the verb: a movie inspired by true events (по мотивам реальных событий). The thing that inspires is inspiring.

entries.meaning: Making you feel sympathy, sadness or tenderness. ---
examples: It was a touching moment when the soldier hugged his daughter.
His letter to his grandmother was very touching.
It's one of the most touching movies I've seen.
entries.position: both — a touching moment, the moment was touching
entries.form: -ing — what causes the feeling
entries.contrast: touching (трогательный) is not touchy (обидчивый): a touching letter, but a touchy subject. The person who feels it is touched.

examples: I was really touched that you remembered my birthday.
She was touched by all the cards from her students.
I've never been more touched by a gift.
Folks in town thought the old man was a little touched.
You'd have to be touched in the head to go out in this storm.

senses.head: Feeling grateful and emotional because someone was kind
examples: I was really touched that you remembered my birthday.
She was touched by all the cards from her students.
I've never been more touched by a gift.

senses.head: Old-fashioned and informal: slightly crazy
examples: Folks in town thought the old man was a little touched.
You'd have to be touched in the head to go out in this storm.

entries.position: predicative only — I was touched, she seemed touched; not before a noun
entries.takes: by + noun: touched by your kindness; that-clause: touched that you remembered; to-infinitive: touched to receive
entries.form: -ed — the person who has the feeling
entries.contrast: Like Russian тронутый, it can mean emotionally moved or, in old-fashioned speech, a little crazy; context makes it clear. It goes only after a verb: I was really touched. The thing that moves you is touching.
